articles.headline: Medora Route Impracticable.
articles.text:
Medora Route Impracticable.

A. J. Maxwell, of the Miles City & Spearfish stage line, informed a Journal reporter that he had a dispatch stating that the proposed stage line between Medora, on the Little Missouri, and Deadwood has been given up, and that an order has been issued to pull off the freighting teams. He also hears that much of the freight is now going to Pierre, and it looks as though the Northwestern railroad has made special rates to get the traffic. Mr. Maxwell stated that the route from Deadwood to Medora is a very hard one, there being thirty miles of very bad lands in one stretch and twenty-five in another, and most of these stretches is full of gumbo, through which hauling is very difficult. A very little rain makes the ground so sticky that it soon clogs the wheels of the wagons.—[Yellowstone Journal.

The above would require no answer, provided all the readers of the article were acquainted with the facts. It has been copied several times, however, and we look for a correction in each case.

The stage line between Medora and Deadwood has not been given up by any means. Those thinking it has, can come here and "go broke" a little easier than in any way we know. The stage company has been fully organized and stages will be run in less than two weeks. It will be started as a tri-weekly and increased to a daily as soon as the rail-road is begun.

That freight is going in by the way of Pierre we do not and have not denied. But will the persons who have been so anxious to defame our route, please answer the following question: "Why is it that all but one or two of the fifty outfits that have loaded here, have come from the Pierre route, where they had constant employment hitherto?" It is a matter of no question that more freight is shipped from here than from Pierre.

The article also states that our route is a very hard one and that there are fifty-five miles of Bad Lands. We would like to know whose word should be taken in this case if it is not that of the freighters themselves. Their testimony is unanimous that it is the best road over which they have ever travelled. We care not what freighter's word is taken, provided he is unprejudiced. Again there are but fifteen miles of Bad Lands on the road and if a man could go over this distance, seeing the road only and having the surrounding country shut out from view, he would never know that he was not on the prairie. The route in the Bad Lands is as level and hard as any well-travelled road.

The article further says that these stretches "is" full of gumbo and a very little rain "makes the ground so sticky that it soon clogs the wheels of the wagons." This is a lie, pure and simple and without a mitigating circumstance. All kinds of weather have been experienced since the route was started. We have personally inquired of nearly every outfit that has come in and the invariable answer has been that there was almost no gumbo and that would not delay freighting a minute except for a little while during the spring thaw and then only for a short distance at the Deadwood end of the route. Bob. Roberts started with the first train that ever went over the route, his and Jos. Pennell's, with not even a bridle path to guide him. He started immediately after a week's steady rain and snow and did not even drop a trail wagon on the whole trip. In spite of all these drawbacks, he made the round trip in shorter time than was ever made from Pierre or any other point into the Hills and return. The weather just previous to this trip was the worst of the season and the time made is a sufficient answer as to the "impracticability" of our route.

And now, whence do all these charges emanate? From one Maxwell who is running a one-horse, buck-board, stage-line(?) from Miles City to Deadwood. Of course from such a source the Medora route is worthless. With the beginning of our route Maxwell will have no farther use for his team or two of cayuses, and his buckboards can be chopped up for kindling wood.

In another article, Maxwell states that he will not come to Medora. Of course he won't, but he forgot to mention the reason. It is that he knows as soon as he shows his nose here, he will be arrested for the larceny of a bateau, stolen from Bly & Co. Considering all the circumstances, it would be as well for Mr. Maxwell to put a bridle on his tongue or be sure he is telling the truth when he turns it loose.
articles.summary: Packard reprints a Yellowstone Journal item quoting A. J. Maxwell that the Medora–Deadwood stage line has been abandoned and the route is impracticable, and rebuts it point by point, accusing Maxwell of stealing a bateau from Bly & Co.

articles.text: A perusal of the statutes calls to light an enactment that is of special interest though comparatively unknown to the farming class of our citizens. It appears that a person planting trees, cuttings or seeds not to exceed twelve feet apart each way on five acres, is exempted from taxes on forty acres of land and improvements not to exceed $1,000, for ten years. The fact of this law should be widely published, as it will do more than anything else to encourage tree planting in Dakota, especially on homesteads.
articles.summary: Notes a Dakota statute exempting tree planters from taxes on forty acres for ten years.

articles.text: The question of representation by the Bad Lands, at the New Orleans exposition, is a subject that should call for immediate action among our citizens. The exposition, in all likelihood, will far outshine that of the Centennial and it is a matter of the greatest importance that our products and natural curiosities should occupy a prominent place. The exposition begins the fifteenth of December and lasts until the fifteenth of May.
articles.summary: Urges the Bad Lands to arrange representation at the New Orleans exposition (Dec. 15 to May 15).

articles.headline: $40.00 Reward.
articles.text:
$40.00 REWARD.

Forty dollars will be paid for the return to Week's ranche, Beaver creek, Montana, of the following stock:

1 bay horse, branded NC, A above, on left shoulder.

1 buckskin pony, branded AIG on right shoulder.

1 buckskin pony, left front foot crooked.

1 sorrel pony.

All the above have hair brand of artist's palette with W in the centre, on left flank. Three of the above had ropes on them. $20.00 reward will be paid for any information leading to their recovery.

Culbertson & Weeks,
Keith, Dawson Co.,
Dak.
articles.summary: Culbertson & Weeks offer $40 for the return of four horses strayed or stolen from Week's ranche on Beaver creek.

articles.text: The per centage of high grade cattle in Kansas is 21, the per cent. for the United States is 18.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipped statistic on high-grade cattle in Kansas.

articles.text: Howard Eaton and Lloyd Roberts came in this morning with a thousand head of cattle for the Badger cattle company.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton and Lloyd Roberts brought in a thousand head of cattle for the Badger cattle company.

articles.text: A cow horn measuring four feet eleven inches in length and eighteen inches around the base is on exhibition at Monticello, Florida, and is supposed to be the largest cow horn in the world.—[N. W. L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped item on a record cow horn in Florida.

articles.text: The colt crop of Colorado will this year number a hundred thousand. Those of thoroughbred will not number a thousand. The large number of this new crop will be of the native variety, and will develop saddle horses on the range.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Colorado's colt crop.

articles.text: Said Mr. Stevens, of Trinidad: "The sheep owners have been getting an unreasonable price for their wool for several years past. From twelve to fifteen cents is a good price for the average quality of the wool produced in Colorado. When the sheep owners were getting eighteen to twenty-two cents per pound, men became so greedy that they sheared their flocks twice a year and then so lazy they left them to freeze and starve through the winter. Prosperity and extortionate prices have spoiled many good men in this country."
articles.summary: Clipped remarks on Colorado wool prices.

articles.text: At a fair calculation the stock-growers of Colorado have invested in bulls yearly, if not quite, $2,000,000. Nine-tenths of all these animals are grades. This is a very expensive necessity to the stock-grower, since the throughbred animals cost him all the way from $200 to $600 each, and the high-grades about $125, and the low grades, those with but a quarter or an eighth of royal blood, about $60 or $75 each. Now, if all the bulls of the State have cost, on an average, $100 each, then the valuation of these brutes will fall not much short of $2,000,000. The cattle-growers will ship about 100,000 head of beeves the present year, and they will have imported in the cycle of the same 5,000 or 10,000 head of high-priced bulls and at least 200,000 stock cattle.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Colorado stockmen's investment in bulls.

articles.text: Each recurring year Texas more nearly approaches the condition of being the nursery and breeding grounds, from which reservoir the western states and territories draw their main supply of young steers. As to this state being the most prolific breeding section, all agree, while many of our successful cattlemen hold that farther north young steers develop into larger beeves than in this latitude. The cry is often heard, "Texas ranches for cows and calves; the western territories for young steers." Well, we can for an indefinite time supply young steers, and stock cattle, too, for less favored breeding grounds. With England opposing the reception of store cattle and Kansas and New Mexico hostile to Texas cattle, from fear of disease, Texans can still raise and fatten beeves profitable for St. Louis and Chicago markets, and for the dead meat markets, both foreign and at home.—[L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Texas as breeding ground for northern ranges.

articles.text: A very short time ago there was a bad outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia near Pittsburg, according to sensational reports that were flung broadcast over the length and breadth of the land, but as soon as proper examination was made it was found that there was no pleuro-pneumonia in the case. Next we had a bad story about foot-and-mouth disease having broken out among the cattle away up in Montana, but it now turns out that there was nothing worse than frozen feet in this case. Not a great while ago a bull calf was found to be suffering with pleuro-pneumonia in Baltimore, and he was clandestinely shipped to Chicago or some other point in the West, and neither this calf nor the two scotchmen that started the foot-and-mouth disease in Kansas in the early spring have as yet been run down and corralled. The talk about pleuro-pneumonia in New York just now is no doubt a certain kind of filthy stable disease that has been common in and around New York for the past forty years and will be the next forty.—[Drover's Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item dismissing cattle-disease scare reports.

articles.text: Mr. [Freuen?] thinks that 60,000 head of cattle from Colorado, Wyoming and the northwest will this year take the northern route; travel through Canada from Duluth, down the St. Lawrence, landing as feeders in England, Ireland and Scotland.—[N. W. L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped estimate of cattle shipped to Britain by the northern route.

articles.text: The excitement over the drive is increasing. It is said that Seth Mabry will bet that 650,000 cattle will cross Red river, and there is a man in San Antonio who will put up all he has that 800,000 will leave Texas between February and August.—[Texas Live Stock Indicator.
articles.summary: Clipped item on the size of the Texas cattle drive.

articles.text: The live stock interests of the northwest received a wounderful impetus this spring. From many of our exchanges throughout this state and Dakota we note that good blooded stock is being purchased from reliable breeders and importers, and the improvements in grades will be the means of increasing the value of our stock to a very large extent.—[Minnesota Farmer.
articles.summary: Clipped item on blooded stock purchases in the northwest.

articles.text: Continual improvement in a herd should be the center pillar in the stockmen's temple, and the one upon which all transactions should be based. The secret; it should be no secret; of success is in paying special attention to the steps that will bring about results that will be most durable. Do not be governed by advice that will profit for a little while and finally bring about disaster and ruin to the herd, but unite good, sound judgment with a few good high grade or thoroughbred bulls, and the greatest proof of success will be success.—[Arizona Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped advice on herd improvement.

articles.text: Cattle raising and agriculture as practiced in the west have about as much affinity for each other as oil and water. It is impossible to have them exist together here in anything like amicable relations, owing to the almost total lack of fences. At present, the herd law in Dakota is oppressive to the cattlemen, although but one or two direct conflicts of interests have as yet arisen. The absence of the herd law would be as oppressive to the farmer. A simple and in fact the only remedy we know, is to set off the western tier of counties or so much of them as is only fit for cattle, as a cattle country and therefore exempt from the herd law. The Bad Lands is not an agricultural country and never will be. It is, however, one of the best cattle countries in the world. Where then, is the justice in having a strictly agricultural law applied to a strictly cattle country. Unless the above plan is adopted, the time is surely coming when serious trouble will arise between the agricultural and cattle interests and the sooner the matter is settled, the better for all concerned. As soon as our cattle organization is effected, this is one of the first and most important matters for it to consider.
articles.summary: Packard argues the western counties should be exempted from the Dakota herd law as a cattle country, a matter for the coming cattle organization.

articles.text:
Europe is at the present day consuming a very much larger amount of animal food than in former times, while its own means of supplying its population is being considerably diminished. For although the live stock of Europe has in the last twenty years, without doubt, been considerable increased, nevertheless it has been utterly impossible to keep pace with the advance of population and the increasing requirements of the people. The collective amount of horned cattle throughout Europe is estimated at 92,000,000 head, of horses about 36,000,000, of sheep about 200,000,000, and of swine about 46,000,000. While these figures show a decided advance over those of twenty years ago, it must be remembered that the question of European supply does not rest so much upon the amount of live stock as the increase of population and the steadily increasing demand from all classes of the communities.

It appears that Europe's relative strength of live stock, with the exception of swine, has fallen off considerable; that is to say, population has advanced more rapidly than live stock, causing a larger demand to be made on other parts of the world. From this report it appears that the Scandinavian countries and Servia stand in a more favorable position as regards live stock than other parts of Europe. Thus Denmark, ranking first, has 735 head of cattle to 1,000 inhabitants, Servia 609 head, Norway 562 and Sweden 483 head.

As to absolute number of live stock in different countries, Russia stands first as regards all classes of animals, having of cattle, including Poland and Finland, in 1876, no less than 25,000,000 head, 45,000,000 sheep, 10,000,000 swine and 17,000,000 horses. The increase in the last twenty years has been about twenty per cent. in sheep, in cattle and swine only about four per cent, while horses have been stationary. Next comes Germany with 15,000,000 of cattle, sheep 25,000,000, swine 7,000,000, and horses 3,000,000.

Austria, Hungary, France, Great Britain, Holland, Norway and Sweden, follow in the order named with 38,000,000 cattle, 30,500,000 swine, 11,500,000 horses and [61?],000,000 sheep between them.

The object of this valuable report, as the intelligent reader has doubtless observed from these condensed items, is to show the favorable outlook of the future of the live stock industry of our own country, so far as prosperity may be dependent upon foreign demand for animal produce. It shows that, as compared with the increase of population, there has been, in Europe, a decrease in the amount of live stock.—[Henry B. Ryder.
articles.summary: Long clipped report on European livestock numbers and demand for American animal produce.

Bad Lands Cow Boy,

articles.summary: Editorial-page masthead.

articles.text: Several more freight outfits came in yesterday.
articles.summary: More freight outfits arrived in Medora.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper is expected home to-day or to-morrow.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper expected home.

articles.text: C. L. [Brinker?], the N. P. agent here has concluded to stay.
articles.summary: The N. P. agent at Medora has decided to stay.

articles.text: Jim Wishart's outfit arrived yesterday. He will load with time freight.
articles.summary: Jim Wishart's freight outfit arrived to load time freight.

articles.text: A. de Steiger has gone to his claim in McLean county to make improvements.
articles.summary: A. de Steiger left to improve his claim in McLean county.

articles.text: J. Juelf's bull outfit pulled out with 75,000 pounds of freight last Monday morning.
articles.summary: J. Juelf's bull outfit left with 75,000 pounds of freight.

articles.text: Star & Bullock's bull outfit loaded yesterday with 20,000 pounds and pulls out to-morrow.
articles.summary: Star & Bullock's outfit loaded 20,000 pounds.

articles.text: About 165,000 pounds of freight have been shipped from Medora to the Hills so far this week.
articles.summary: About 165,000 pounds of freight shipped from Medora to the Black Hills this week.

articles.text: Work is progressing fast on the new side-track and inside of a fortnight the steel will be laid.
articles.summary: Work on the new side-track is progressing.

articles.text: John O'Sullivan is building a barber shop on his lot next to John Warn's temperance tabernacle.
articles.summary: John O'Sullivan is building a barber shop.

articles.text: M. M. Coleman and C. F. Brown have bought a lot and intend erecting a building for a boarding house.
articles.summary: Coleman and Brown bought a lot for a boarding house.

articles.text: The only and original General P. D. Q. Sheridan will hereafter attend to the cuisine of the Hotel de Mores.
articles.summary: 'General P. D. Q. Sheridan' to cook at the Hotel de Mores.

articles.text: Whitehead's, Thorn's, Gaar's, Dexter's, and Magre's, outfits all loaded this week with time freight and pulled out for the Hills.
articles.summary: Five freight outfits loaded and left for the Hills.

articles.text: The coal in the butte east of town has developed an unexpected superiority and the quantity is sufficient to last for ages.
articles.summary: Coal in the butte east of town proves of superior quality.

articles.text: Rassie Deffebach returned last night from Mattock's ranch, having accompanied Clark's herd of bulls that far on the road.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffebach returned from Mattock's ranch after accompanying Clark's bulls.

articles.text: Ferris & Merrifield have gone to Iowa to purchase a thousand more cattle for their ranch. They expect to return in a month or six weeks.
articles.summary: Ferris & Merrifield went to Iowa to buy a thousand more cattle.

articles.text: Thorn's outfit arrived last Saturday at ten in the morning and before three in the afternoon was loaded and pulling back for the Hills.
articles.summary: Thorn's outfit arrived and reloaded in five hours.

articles.text: As we set these lines, No. 2 is pulling in, over sixteen hours late. The cause of the delay was the washing away of the bridge at Gallatin.
articles.summary: Train No. 2 arrived over sixteen hours late after the Gallatin bridge washed out.

articles.text: Tom Matthews is kept busy in his new position of stock inspector at Mandan. We notice by the papers that he has been testing the tender-footedness of some of the editors.
articles.summary: Tom Matthews busy as stock inspector at Mandan.

articles.text: Graham's mule outfit arrived yesterday morning. Mr. Graham was one of the first to pull over our route and pronounces the cut-off road the best he ever freighted over.
articles.summary: Graham's mule outfit arrived; Graham praises the cut-off road.

articles.text: An application for the granting of a charter for the establishment of a Masonic lodge has been forwarded to the proper official and it is thought that the request will be granted.
articles.summary: Application forwarded for a Masonic lodge charter.

articles.text: A number of improvements have taken place at the slaughter house. A large quantity of stone has arrived and a new foundation for the cold-storage end will be built immediately.
articles.summary: Improvements at the slaughter house, including a new cold-storage foundation.

articles.text: The pillow-slip dance given by the young ladies at the Pyramid Park hotel last Friday night was all that was expected. It was a jolly crowd, intent on having a jolly time and they had it.
articles.summary: Pillow-slip dance at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: The freighters who started off to pick up buffalo bones have not had the success they expected. The most of them will make but one load of bones and then return to freighting.
articles.summary: Buffalo-bone gathering proved disappointing for freighters.

articles.text: Mrs. T. G. Jones and son George, arrived last night from Billings. They will start on for Spearfish to-morrow or next day. Mrs. Jones will probably invest in several valuable lots before leaving.
articles.summary: Mrs. T. G. Jones and son arrived from Billings en route to Spearfish.

articles.text: Some of these times the railroad company will get itself into trouble by running trains out ahead of time. Every train carrying passengers is obliged by law to wait at each station until the advertised time for leaving.
articles.summary: Complaint about trains leaving ahead of time.

articles.text: Peter Book is now making pressed brick and they are as much of a success as the common brick. They are and are claimed to be the best brick made in Dakota and Mr. Book is anxious for competition both as to quality and price.
articles.summary: Peter Book now making pressed brick.

articles.text: Some despicable spotter, in order to hold his job, trumped up charges against conductors Clark and Hutton and as a consequence they are laid off. It will be a long while before the road gets two better or more popular conductors.
articles.summary: Conductors Clark and Hutton laid off on a spotter's charges.

articles.text: E. I. Goodkind, of the Bismarck firm of Wise & Goodkind was in town Monday and Tuesday. The firm's advertisement, appearing in this issue of the Cow Boy, shows the liberal spirit that has built them up such a large and profitable trade.
articles.summary: E. I. Goodkind of Wise & Goodkind visited Medora.

articles.text: Mr. Rosevelt is still at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch, hunting and playing cowboy. It seems to be more congenial work than reforming New York state politics. He is thoroughly impressed with the profit of raising cattle in the Bad Lands, as his vigorous backing of Ferris Bros. & Merrifield testifies.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt still at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch hunting and backing the firm.

articles.text: A letter from Star & Bullock makes known the fact that the shipping of a consignment of their goods by the way of Pierre, was a straight steal on the part of the North-Western. The whole consignment was billed via Medora, and was switched off to Pierre. There is a great consolation in the fact that the North-Western company did not haul a pound of the freight from Pierre and may in the end have to pay the charges themselves.
articles.summary: Star & Bullock goods billed via Medora were diverted to Pierre by the North-Western.

articles.text: W. M. Brewer, late editor of the Minnesela Boomer, came in last Saturday from Deadwood. Mr. Brewer has had a large experience both at freighting and staging and pronounces this route to be altogether the best one running into the Hills. We are pleased to state that Mr. Brewer intends settling in Medora and going into business.
articles.summary: W. M. Brewer arrived from Deadwood and plans to settle in Medora.

articles.text: The work on the new billiard hall and theatre building is about completed, the hard-finish coat being the only thing to finish. The house-warming and opening dance will probably be put off until the glorious fourth. Some of the furniture has already arrived and Pennell & Roberts intend sparing no expense in fitting up the building.
articles.summary: New billiard hall and theatre building of Pennell & Roberts nearly done; opening probably July 4.

articles.text: The N. P. time table will soon be changed so as to make the trips between St. Paul and Portland and return in six hours faster time. This will make No. 1's time about four in the afternoon and No. 2's about five in the morning. The trains now run just right for free rides across the river but the boys will have to count ties after the change.
articles.summary: N. P. time table to change soon.

articles.text: Lieutenant Varnum has completed the official survey of a route from Dickinson to Fort Meade and is now working on the survey of the Belfield route. As soon as this is finished he will come to Medora and survey the route from here. Owing to the shortness of our line and the many improvements made upon it, it is not hard to prophecy which route will be finally chosen.
articles.summary: Lt. Varnum surveying Black Hills routes; will survey from Medora.

articles.text: L. H. Palmer, of Deadwood, arrived yesterday. He is an energetic business man, owning considerable property in Deadwood. He has the utmost faith in the future of Medora, and it gives us pleasure to note the fact that he intends settling here and putting up business houses for rent. He says that the freight route is all and more than has been claimed for it, it being the best he has ever seen.
articles.summary: L. H. Palmer of Deadwood arrived and plans to build business houses in Medora.

articles.text: A glance at our cattle-cut columns will prove that the cattlemen appreciate the value of advertising as well as other business men. At no distant date we expect to publish every cattle brand in the Bad Lands. Although the change of cuts necessitated a large expense, we are more than repaid by many congratulatory remarks on the improvement, and the substantial way in which cattle and horse men are bringing in their brands for publication. A number of cow-boys have made clippings of the brands, pasting them in small books for handy reference. It is an excellent thing to do and will soon familiarize anyone with the different brands.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy notes growth of its cattle-brand advertising.

articles.headline: Notice of Dissolution.
articles.text:
NOTICE OF DISSOLUTION.

To All Whom It May Concern: Be it known that on and after this 24th day of May, 1884, the partnership heretofore existing between Chas. Shaffer and John Munroe, under the firm name of Shaffer & Munroe, Plum Grove ranch, on the Little Missouri river, is dissolved by mutual consent. All indebtedness of the firm to date will be paid by John Munroe.
articles.summary: Notice that the Shaffer & Munroe partnership at Plum Grove ranch was dissolved May 24, 1884.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Theodore Roosevelt staying at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported that Roosevelt was still at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch, hunting and 'playing cowboy,' impressed with the profit of Bad Lands cattle raising and vigorously backing Ferris Bros. & Merrifield.
events.excerpt: Mr. Rosevelt is still at Ferris & Merrifield's ranch, hunting and playing cowboy.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Ferris & Merrifield go to Iowa to buy cattle
events.summary: Ferris & Merrifield went to Iowa to purchase a thousand more cattle for their ranch, expecting to return in a month or six weeks.
events.excerpt: Ferris & Merrifield have gone to Iowa to purchase a thousand more cattle for their ranch.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Cow Boy rebuts report that Medora–Deadwood stage line is abandoned
events.summary: Answering a Yellowstone Journal item quoting A. J. Maxwell, the paper insisted the Medora–Deadwood stage company was organized and would run tri-weekly stages within two weeks, and defended the freight road as level and free of gumbo.
events.excerpt: The stage company has been fully organized and stages will be run in less than two weeks.

events.date_basis: 'in less than two weeks' from Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Medora–Deadwood stage line to begin running
events.summary: The paper said stages on the Medora–Deadwood line would run in less than two weeks, starting tri-weekly and becoming daily once the railroad was begun.
events.excerpt: It will be started as a tri-weekly and increased to a daily as soon as the rail-road is begun.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Paper accuses A. J. Maxwell of stealing a bateau
events.summary: The Cow Boy said Maxwell would be arrested for larceny of a bateau stolen from Bly & Co. if he came to Medora.
events.excerpt: he will be arrested for the larceny of a bateau, stolen from Bly & Co.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Cattlemen offer $250 reward against grass fires
events.summary: N. P. Ref. Car Co., Continental Cattle Co. and other outfits offered $250 for information leading to the arrest of anyone setting fire to the grass in western Dakota cattle country.
events.excerpt: setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Horses missing from Week's ranche, Beaver creek
events.summary: Culbertson & Weeks offered $40 for the return of four horses, three with ropes on them, to Week's ranche on Beaver creek.
events.excerpt: Forty dollars will be paid for the return to Week's ranche, Beaver creek, Montana

events.date_basis: 'this morning' in Thu 19 Jun 1884 issue
events.title: Eaton and Roberts bring in a thousand cattle for the Badger company
events.summary: Howard Eaton and Lloyd Roberts came in with a thousand head of cattle for the Badger cattle company.
events.excerpt: Howard Eaton and Lloyd Roberts came in this morning with a thousand head of cattle for the Badger cattle company.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Cow Boy calls for exempting cattle country from herd law
events.summary: Packard argued that the western tier of counties, fit only for cattle, should be exempted from the Dakota herd law to avoid conflict between farmers and cattlemen.
events.excerpt: The Bad Lands is not an agricultural country and never will be.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884
events.title: Call for Bad Lands exhibit at New Orleans exposition
events.summary: The paper urged immediate action to represent the Bad Lands' products and natural curiosities at the New Orleans exposition.
events.excerpt: our products and natural curiosities should occupy a prominent place

events.date_basis: 'yesterday' before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: Several more freight outfits came in.
events.excerpt: Several more freight outfits came in yesterday.

events.excerpt: A. de Steiger has gone to his claim in McLean county

events.excerpt: J. Juelf's bull outfit pulled out with 75,000 pounds of freight last Monday morning.

events.excerpt: About 165,000 pounds of freight have been shipped from Medora to the Hills so far this week.

events.summary: Work was progressing on the new side-track, with steel to be laid within a fortnight.
events.excerpt: inside of a fortnight the steel will be laid.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: John O'Sullivan was building a barber shop next to John Warn's temperance tabernacle.
events.excerpt: John O'Sullivan is building a barber shop

events.excerpt: have bought a lot and intend erecting a building for a boarding house.

events.excerpt: will hereafter attend to the cuisine of the Hotel de Mores.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: The coal in the butte east of town was reported of unexpected quality and great quantity.
events.excerpt: The coal in the butte east of town has developed an unexpected superiority

events.excerpt: Rassie Deffebach returned last night from Mattock's ranch

events.excerpt: before three in the afternoon was loaded and pulling back for the Hills.

events.date_basis: 'as we set these lines' at press time for Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.excerpt: No. 2 is pulling in, over sixteen hours late.

events.date_basis: 'yesterday morning' before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: Graham, one of the first to use the route, arrived and called the cut-off road the best he had freighted over.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: An application for a charter for a Masonic lodge was forwarded.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: Freighters who went to pick up buffalo bones found less success than expected and planned to return to freighting.

events.summary: E. I. Goodkind of Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, was in town.
events.excerpt: was in town Monday and Tuesday.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.date_basis: 'last Saturday' before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: W. M. Brewer, late editor of the Minnesela Boomer, arrived from Deadwood, praised the route and planned to go into business in Medora.
events.excerpt: Mr. Brewer intends settling in Medora and going into business.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: Pennell & Roberts's new billiard hall and theatre building was about completed.
events.excerpt: The work on the new billiard hall and theatre building is about completed

events.summary: The house-warming and opening dance would probably be held on the Fourth of July.
events.excerpt: The house-warming and opening dance will probably be put off until the glorious fourth.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: The N. P. planned a faster schedule, moving No. 1 to about 4 p.m. and No. 2 to about 5 a.m.
events.excerpt: This will make No. 1's time about four in the afternoon

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: Lieutenant Varnum finished surveying a Dickinson–Fort Meade route, was surveying the Belfield route, and would next survey from Medora.
events.excerpt: As soon as this is finished he will come to Medora and survey the route from here.

events.date_basis: 'yesterday' before Thu 19 Jun 1884

events.summary: L. H. Palmer, a Deadwood property owner, arrived and planned to settle and build business houses for rent in Medora.
events.excerpt: he intends settling here and putting up business houses for rent.

events.summary: The paper said cattlemen were bringing in brands for publication and it hoped to publish every brand in the Bad Lands.
